subject: Career
title: The Anchoring Effect in Offers
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Anchoring Effect in Offers.

hook.text: They offer $85K. Now every counter you make revolves around $85K. You've been anchored.

buildup.text: The first number in any negotiation disproportionately shapes the final outcome.

discovery.text: If you can name your number first with a justification, you set the anchor instead.

twist.text: But anchoring too high without data feels delusional. The anchor must be backed by evidence.

climax.text: 'Based on market data, I'm targeting $105K-$115K.' — specific, defensible, and high.

punchline.text: Set the anchor or live inside theirs.

quiz.question: What is the anchoring effect in negotiation?
options: The first number shapes the entire range
The final offer is always the anchor

details.summary: Anchoring is a cognitive bias in which the first number mentioned in a negotiation disproportionately influences the final outcome. Whoever sets the initial salary figure frames the entire discussion, making the opening number one of the most powerful tools in compensation talks.
details.whyItMatters: Research shows final agreements cluster within ten to fifteen percent of the anchor. Controlling the anchor can shift your outcome by thousands of dollars.
takeaways: The first number stated shapes the entire negotiation
Higher anchors consistently yield higher final outcomes
Always back your anchor with market data to maintain credibility

faq.question: Should I always state my salary expectations first?
faq.answer: When you have solid market data, naming the first number lets you set the anchor on your terms. If you lack information, prompting the employer to share their range first prevents you from anchoring below your actual market value.

faq.question: How do I counter an anchor that feels unreasonably low?
faq.answer: Present an evidence-based counter-anchor rather than reacting emotionally. Cite specific market data, comparable offers, or industry salary surveys to reframe the discussion and move the reference point upward.
